sections.title: Profile
sections.text: Claiming to be a descendant of an Iberian Royal Navy admiral and a member of the fallen noble de Toledo family, she has gathered a large following of supporters across Iberia. However, because the history this Operator recounted seriously contradicts the Inquisition's records, her profession was classified as freelance when HR re-registered her. De Toledo joined Rhodes Island on the recommendation of Operator Irene. Her eloquence and knowledge of Iberia are sufficient to assist the Operators of the Iberia Office with basic work.

sections.title: Clinical Analysis
sections.text:
Imaging tests reveal clear, normal outlines of internal organs, and no abnormal shadows have been detected. Originium granules have not been detected in the circulatory system and there is no sign of infection. At this time, this operator is believed to be uninfected.

[Cell-Originium Assimilation] 0%
Operator de Toledo shows no signs of Originium infection.

[Blood Originium-Crystal Density] 0.12u/L
Operator de Toledo rarely comes into contact with Originium, but her physical examination report still shows several abnormal indicators: dehydration, anemia, long-term malnutrition... It can be inferred that her past wandering across Iberia was very harsh. The Medical Department will continue to monitor this Operator's basic health.

"...Of course I understand medical records are your private information, and we'll archive them according to standard procedure, but asking us to encrypt this report is a bit..."
"No, no, no, you don't get it at all. As a noble, I can't let anyone, especially my supporters, know I'm malnourished! Who wants to follow a leader who can't even feed herself? Hey, wait... maybe this is a new angle? Willing to suffer so her supporters can live well... sounds like it'd win even more hearts, doesn't it? Fine, no encryption then!"

sections.title: Archive File 1
sections.text:
[Operator de Toledo profile archiving record]
Archive File 1
Current status: Not filed
Annotation: HR Operator, please speed up the background check and confirm the authenticity of all of Operator de Toledo's records. In special circumstances, you may interview the Operator herself or people associated with her and confirm the records based on their oral accounts.

Archive File 1
Current status: Returned
Annotation: I know organizing three oral accounts of six hours each is difficult, but pure audio files really don't meet the archive submission format. Also, when converting them into documents, please take care not to copy over grandiose expressions such as "Conquerors of the Sea, the de Toledo family of supreme glory."

Archive File 1
Current status: Returned again
Annotation: By regulation, the background check should have been finished three months ago—fine, HR Operator, I do sympathize with you. Getting a single true word about her origins out of Tefi really is far too hard.
Reply: Senior... who's Tefi?
Reply: It's Operator de Toledo's nickname. Strange, you haven't heard her mention it in these four months? Wait, you've never heard her tell "Rea-Iberia and the Visitor from the Sea"? What about "The Officer's Last Snowy Night Before Death"?
Reply: Huh...?

That was the first time in my life I'd heard a speech so impassioned, so moving, and so off-the-wall. Operator de Toledo stood in the middle of the sunken lounge in the activity room and told three stories to Operators unfamiliar with Iberia and to people receiving treatment on Rhodes Island. Honestly, she sounded like a complete con artist; probably only the kids in the front row holding toy sailboats and paper badges fell for it. Oh, and the activity room really has too few seats; standing for three hours straight is bad for your back—fine, I admit it, I was a little moved by this flamboyant Liberi too, and I even pulled out my wallet when she asked for "Golden Fleet preparation funds." To be fair, that's not falling for it. Many in the audience, myself included, were probably moved by the Iberian stories she told, not because we truly believed she was some illustrious noble. Besides, she seems to treat her supporters well; she didn't even make them do the sound effects for her speech, handling it all herself.
Unfortunately, three hours later, I still couldn't tell which lines in Operator de Toledo's stories were true, and I may never finish archiving her profile. But I think I did figure out one thing: I'm not suited to being an HR Operator who records and checks facts. I should pursue the creative dream I set aside long ago. I will join de Toledo's ranks as a clerk and write some stories for her. By the time the next HR Operator comes to verify her profile, perhaps I'll be able to tell them what kind of person de Toledo really is.
—Attachment to a letter of resignation, from a former HR Operator

sections.title: Archive File 2
sections.text:
Whenever Operator de Toledo completes a mission for the Iberia Office and returns to Rhodes Island with her supporters, they patrol the base calling themselves the 'Rhodes Island Navy.'
Calling it a patrol, it's more like a kind of sightseeing. De Toledo calls the Operator dormitories her "royal chambers," the recuperation courtyard her "garden," and the Engineering Department her "armaments factory," drawing no small amount of criticism. De Toledo pays no heed at all to what others think of her. She had a child used to sleeping on damp floors in Iberia lie on her own soft mattress; she helped a gravely ill elder to the recuperation courtyard to smell flowers not found by the sea; and as for those timid young people who could nonetheless build sturdy things, de Toledo shoved them straight into the Engineering Department. Three days later, the eyes of both the young people and the Engineering Operators were shining, and they introduced their newly invented devices even more long-windedly than she does. Over time, the voices complaining of de Toledo's high-handed behavior vanished, along with the letters complaining about her taking over the activity room. Anyone who has dealt with her comes to understand: de Toledo does as much as she says. Given how very much she says, what she does for her supporters is enough to make one temporarily forget that her "supporters" are in fact "victims" who fell for her act—

Victims? I don't understand... Lady de Toledo isn't a storm, so how could we be 'victimized' by her? I followed her all the way here from Finridge Town with nothing to my name, and she put me in charge of cooking, making seaweed soup for everyone. Of course, we can't always gather enough seaweed, so we mix in a bit of sand. She said that once she finds a reliable patron, or has an estate of her own, she'll take us all there and we'll drink seaweed soup with nothing but seaweed in it. I know this place isn't her home, but I got my soup in a place full of tables and chairs, so Lady de Toledo didn't lie to me. What? Her identity? Sometimes she really doesn't seem much like a noble, but then, we don't know what Iberian nobles are actually like either, do we? If those noble lords already buried in the ground had been like her, it would have been quite fine. Ah, I remember now: there was a supporter who doubted her before, and she proved her noble lineage to us. The naval uniform? No, not that. Did you know she has eleven toes?
—A supporter of de Toledo, an ordinary elderly Iberian, stopping the archivist to speak

sections.title: Archive File 3
sections.text:
"On the Hereditary Lineage of the de Toledo Family and Its Eleven Toes"
Esteban Enríquez de Toledo, Royal Navy admiral of Iberia's Golden Age. Resolute in character and fiercely proud, he was an outstanding helmsman and navigator, called "de Toledo the Wave-Turner" by the Iberians of his time. Of his eighty-three years, he spent nearly seventy at sea; no matter how fierce the storm his ship faced, he would always stand at the very front of the deck. Countless sailors took him as their model, and their extreme imitation sharply raised both the death rate and the promotion rate of sailors at the time.
However, after the Great Silence, Rea-Iberia sank, and a great deal of material on the royal family and nobility was lost. Memories passed down by word of mouth and the few surviving records revealed another, little-known side of this noble. Esteban Enríquez de Toledo suffered from hereditary polydactyly, and his malformed extra toes made him limp when walking on level ground, while the rocking of a ship conveniently masked this defect. His mastery of seafaring may have been natural talent, or perhaps it was the fruit of his efforts to hide his disability for the sake of his pride.
The same tragedy befell his descendants. His heir, Estanislao, became an outstanding naval admiral, and had it not been for the Great Silence, he too would have spent his whole life at sea like his father. Rumor has it that when the Great Silence came, he leapt from his ship, limped his way out of Rea-Iberia, and vanished without a trace.
Now, Estefanía Colón de Toledo, who claims to be the great-granddaughter of Esteban Enríquez de Toledo, has reappeared. Her naval uniform and eleven toes alike attest to her identity. We ought to follow in her footsteps and restore the glory of the Iberian Royal Navy...

[A note tucked between the pages of a book]
I never expected that after I resigned from HR, the first task de Toledo would give me was to write her biography. Then again, there have always been plenty of supporters doubting her noble status. Most of the above was excerpted from stories she told and then logically strung back together. I am quite certain de Toledo is not a descendant of that great admiral, but I was genuinely curious whether she really has eleven toes, and if not, how she fooled the supporters who demanded proof. On the fourth day after the question arose, I found the answer in another of her stories. Perhaps this too is a tale she made up based on Iberian reality, but I'll record it for now:
There was once a poor Iberian woman whose husband had been swallowed by the sea, and she awaited childbirth alone. During delivery, the baby was in the wrong position, and its feet came out first. That unfortunate child also suffered from polydactyly, and the deeply devout woman, believing she had given birth to a Sea Terror, fainted. The child turned out fine, but the woman took her own life. The child was raised by the villagers, but her extra toes kept her from doing physical labor. She left the village, and no one knows what became of her after that.

sections.title: Archive File 4
sections.text:
[Activity log of an Operator dispatched to the Iberia Office]
Before formally working with Operator de Toledo, I had quite a few complaints about the way she did things. Never mind that she brings a huge crowd of supporters wherever she goes and clears her throat to start a speech whenever there's a bit of open space; before every mission, this restless Liberi would vanish completely. Whenever I couldn't be sure whether acting a certain way was appropriate by Iberian custom, our nominal 'guide' was basically never by our side.
Ever since Rea-Iberia returned to the Iberian coastline and the Inquisition decided to lift Iberia's blockade, our work has become harder than ever. As the legacy of the Golden Age gradually returns to people's lives, Iberian faith is being restructured. Some of the populace no longer obey the doctrines promulgated by the Inquisition without question, while on the other side, those whose lives were shaped by faith claim they have been "betrayed." Once, a fasting Iberian refused our help outright, reciting old scripture to drive us away, so we left. Half an hour later, a furious de Toledo appeared before us.
That was the first time I saw de Toledo angry. I had once seen her wandering near that commoner's wooden hut; perhaps he was one of her potential supporters. But she just handed me a list with dozens of names on it, half of them already crossed out. She told me that one of her supporters was this town's sugar distributor, who every afternoon brought raw sugar out from the sugarcane farm and delivered a little to each person on the list. The wish he made to the great noble de Toledo was that he would no longer have to cross out names on the list.
On the second day, de Toledo set up a small podium at the door of that Iberian's house. On the third day, she spoke for ten hours straight, and just as the sun was about to disappear beyond the sea, the Iberian behind the door answered her with a single remark. On the fourth day, she used her so-called "family motto" to "bless" some raw sugar. It was neither one thing nor the other, but the man licked the sugar on the plate. With that, our assistance mission came to a successful end, and she gained a loyal supporter.
On the way back to Rhodes Island, I apologized to her and at the same time congratulated de Toledo on another addition to her ranks. She didn't pat my arm and laugh it off as usual. She looked at the supporters crowded around her. They called her the noblest person in Iberia, a title that until then had belonged, in their mouths, to the saints of the Inquisition.
I think I understand what she's worried about. In an Iberia still in turmoil, she needs to be 'the noble de Toledo'; she needs to give the 'betrayed' Iberians a choice. Perhaps only when most Iberians can believe in themselves will she choose to stop deceiving.

sections.title: Promotion Record
sections.text:
"Ahem... Minutes of the third meeting on cooperation between the de Toledo Naval Reserve and Rhodes Island..."
"Doctor, can this little thing really record all our conversations? Hey, wait, you didn't have it recording when I was secretly telling you the truth too, did you?"
"Yes, yes, the recording's on right now, and everything I'm saying is the truth, all of it!"
"Back to the matter at hand: this meeting is to report on the preparations of the Naval Reserve I've organized, funded by Rhodes Island."
"Recruitment, naval training, and weapons manufacturing are all progressing steadily, and the outlook is very optimistic. I propose increasing the investment—hey, don't pull up the activity logs!"
“……”
"Don't just go quiet on me. How is rescuing two kids from human traffickers not recruitment? How is rowing out to gather seaweed not naval training? And weapons manufacturing—hand cannons and swords are only useful in the hands of the Inquisition. Our weapons should be plows and shovels!"
"I have to let my supporters live properly first before I can think about anything else. Trust me, I may con people, but I never break my word!"
"Doctor, you agree to increase the investment? There's one condition?"
"...You want to weave my experiences with my supporters into a story for the speeches too?"
"No problem! I promise you, you'll definitely be the first to hear it!"
